{{Short description|Monotone maps have countable discontinuities}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2024}}
{{technical|date=May 2025}}
In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] field of [[mathematical analysis|analysis]], a well-known theorem describes the set of [[Discontinuity (mathematics)|discontinuities]] of a [[Monotonic function#Monotonicity in calculus and analysis|monotone]] [[real-valued function]] of a real variable; all discontinuities of such a (monotone) function are necessarily [[Jump discontinuity|jump discontinuities]] and there are at most [[Countable set|countably many]] of them.

Usually, this theorem appears in literature without a name. It is called '''Froda's theorem''' in some recent works; in his 1929 dissertation, [[Alexandru Froda]] stated that the result was previously well-known and had provided his own [[elementary proof]] for the sake of convenience.<ref>{{cite thesis|first=Alexandre|last= Froda|title=Sur la distribution des propriétés de voisinage des functions de variables réelles|url= http://www.numdam.org/item/THESE_1929__102__1_0.pdf|publisher= Hermann|location= Paris|date= 3 December 1929| jfm=55.0742.02}}</ref> Prior work on discontinuities had already been discussed in the 1875 memoir of the French mathematician [[Jean Gaston Darboux]].<ref>[[Jean Gaston Darboux]], [http://archive.numdam.org/ARCHIVE/ASENS/ASENS_1875_2_4_/ASENS_1875_2_4__57_0/ASENS_1875_2_4__57_0.pdf Mémoire sur les fonctions discontinues], [[Annales Scientifiques de l'École Normale Supérieure]], 2-ème série, t. IV, 1875, Chap VI.</ref>

== Definitions ==

Denote the [[limit from the left]] by
<math display=block>f\left(x^-\right) := \lim_{z \nearrow x} f(z) = \lim_{\stackrel{h \to 0}{h > 0}} f(x-h)</math>
and denote the [[limit from the right]] by
<math display=block>f\left(x^+\right) := \lim_{z \searrow x} f(z) = \lim_{\stackrel{h \to 0}{h > 0}} f(x+h).</math>

If <math>f\left(x^+\right)</math> and <math>f\left(x^-\right)</math> exist and are finite then the difference <math>f\left(x^+\right) - f\left(x^-\right)</math> is called the ''' jump'''{{sfn|Nicolescu|Dinculeanu|Marcus|1971|p=213}} of <math>f</math> at <math>x.</math>

Consider a real-valued function <math>f</math> of real variable <math>x</math> defined in a neighborhood of a point <math>x.</math> If <math>f</math> is discontinuous at the point <math>x</math> then the discontinuity will be a '''[[removable discontinuity]]''', or an '''[[essential discontinuity]]''', or a '''[[jump discontinuity]]''' (also called a '''discontinuity of the first kind''').{{sfn|Rudin|1964|loc=Def. 4.26, pp. 81–82}}
If the function is continuous at <math>x</math> then the jump at <math>x</math> is zero. Moreover, if <math>f</math> is not continuous at <math>x,</math> the jump can be zero at <math>x</math> if <math>f\left(x^+\right) = f\left(x^-\right) \neq f(x).</math>

== Precise statement ==

Let <math>f</math> be a real-valued [[Monotonic function#Monotonicity in calculus and analysis|monotone]] function defined on an [[Interval (mathematics)#Notations for intervals|interval]] <math>I.</math> Then the set of discontinuities of the first kind is [[Countable set|at most countable]].

One can prove{{sfn|Rudin|1964|loc=Corollary, p. 83}}{{sfn|Nicolescu|Dinculeanu|Marcus|1971|p=213}} that all points of discontinuity of a monotone real-valued function defined on an interval are jump discontinuities and hence, by our definition, of the first kind. With this remark the theorem takes the stronger form:

Let <math>f</math> be a monotone function defined on an interval <math>I.</math> Then the set of discontinuities is at most countable.

== Proofs ==

This proof starts by proving the special case where the function's domain is a closed and bounded interval <math>[a, b].</math>{{sfn|Apostol|1957|pp=162–3}}{{sfn|Hobson|1907|p=245}} The proof of the general case follows from this special case.

=== Proof when the domain is closed and bounded ===

Two proofs of this special case are given.

==== Proof 1 ====

Let <math>I := [a, b]</math> be an interval and let <math>f : I \to \R</math> be a non-decreasing function (such as an [[Monotonic function|increasing]] function).
Then for any <math>a < x < b,</math>
<math display=block>f(a) ~\leq~ f\left(a^+\right) ~\leq~ f\left(x^-\right) ~\leq~ f\left(x^+\right) ~\leq~ f\left(b^-\right) ~\leq~ f(b).</math>
Let <math>\alpha > 0</math> and let <math>x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_n</math> be <math>n</math> points inside <math>I</math> at which the jump of <math>f</math> is greater or equal to <math>\alpha</math>:
<math display=block>f\left(x_i^+\right) - f\left(x_i^-\right) \geq \alpha,\ i=1,2,\ldots,n</math>

For any <math>i=1,2,\ldots,n,</math> <math>f\left(x_i^+\right) \leq f\left(x_{i+1}^-\right)</math> so that <math>f\left(x_{i+1}^-\right) - f\left(x_i^+\right) \geq 0.</math>
Consequently,
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{9}
f(b) - f(a)
&\geq f\left(x_n^+\right) - f\left(x_1^-\right) \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n \left[f\left(x_i^+\right) - f\left(x_i^-\right)\right] + \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \left[f\left(x_{i+1}^-\right) - f\left(x_i^+\right)\right] \\
&\geq \sum_{i=1}^n \left[f\left(x_i^+\right) - f\left(x_i^-\right)\right] \\
&\geq n \alpha
\end{alignat}</math>
and hence <math>n \leq \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{\alpha}.</math>

Since <math>f(b) - f(a) < \infty</math> we have that the number of points at which the jump is greater than <math>\alpha</math> is finite (possibly even zero).

Define the following sets:
<math display=block>S_1: = \left\{x : x \in I, f\left(x^+\right) - f\left(x^-\right) \geq 1\right\},</math>
<math display=block>S_n: = \left\{x : x \in I, \frac{1}{n} \leq f\left(x^+\right) - f\left(x^-\right) < \frac{1}{n-1}\right\},\ n\geq 2.</math>

Each set <math>S_n</math> is finite or the [[empty set]]. The union
<math>S = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty S_n</math> contains all points at which the jump is positive and hence contains all points of discontinuity. Since every <math>S_i,\ i=1,2,\ldots</math> is at most countable, their union <math>S</math> is also at most countable.

If <math>f</math> is non-increasing (or [[Monotonic function|decreasing]]) then the proof is similar. This completes the proof of the special case where the function's domain is a closed and bounded interval.
<math>\blacksquare</math>

==== Proof 2 ====

For a monotone function <math>f</math>, let <math>f\nearrow</math> mean that <math>f</math> is monotonically non-decreasing and let <math>f\searrow</math> mean that <math>f</math> is monotonically non-increasing. Let <math>f : [a, b] \to \R</math> is a monotone function and let <math>D</math> denote the set of all points <math>d \in [a, b]</math> in the domain of <math>f</math> at which <math>f</math> is discontinuous (which is necessarily a jump discontinuity).

Because <math>f</math> has a jump discontinuity at <math>d \in D,</math> <math>f\left(d^-\right) \neq f\left(d^+\right)</math> so there exists some [[rational number]] <math>y_d \in \Q</math> that lies strictly in between <math>f\left(d^-\right) \text{ and } f\left(d^+\right)</math> (specifically, if <math>f \nearrow</math> then pick <math>y_d \in \Q</math> so that <math>f\left(d^-\right) < y_d < f\left(d^+\right)</math> while if <math>f \searrow</math> then pick <math>y_d \in \Q</math> so that <math>f\left(d^-\right) > y_d > f\left(d^+\right)</math> holds).

It will now be shown that if <math>d, e \in D</math> are distinct, say with <math>d < e,</math> then <math>y_d \neq y_e.</math>
If <math>f \nearrow</math> then <math>d < e</math> implies <math>f\left(d^+\right) \leq f\left(e^-\right)</math> so that <math>y_d < f\left(d^+\right) \leq f\left(e^-\right) < y_e.</math>
If on the other hand <math>f \searrow</math> then <math>d < e</math> implies <math>f\left(d^+\right) \geq f\left(e^-\right)</math> so that <math>y_d > f\left(d^+\right) \geq f\left(e^-\right) > y_e.</math>
Either way, <math>y_d \neq y_e.</math>

Thus every <math>d \in D</math> is associated with a unique rational number (said differently, the map <math>D \to \Q</math> defined by <math>d \mapsto y_d</math> is [[Injective function|injective]]).
Since <math>\Q</math> is countable, the same must be true of <math>D.</math>
<math>\blacksquare</math>

=== Proof of general case ===

Suppose that the domain of <math>f</math> (a monotone real-valued function) is equal to a union of countably many closed and bounded intervals; say its domain is <math>\bigcup_{n} \left[a_n, b_n\right]</math> (no requirements are placed on these closed and bounded intervals{{efn|So for instance, these intervals need not be [[Disjoint sets|pairwise disjoint]] nor is it required that they intersect only at endpoints. It is even possible that <math>\left[a_n, b_n\right] \subseteq \left[a_{n+1}, b_{n+1}\right]</math> for all <math>n</math>}}).
It follows from the special case proved above that for every index <math>n,</math> the [[Restriction of a map|restriction]] <math>f\big\vert_{\left[a_n, b_n\right]} : \left[a_n, b_n\right] \to \R</math> of <math>f</math> to the interval <math>\left[a_n, b_n\right]</math> has at most countably many discontinuities; denote this (countable) set of discontinuities by <math>D_n.</math>
If <math>f</math> has a discontinuity at a point <math>x_0 \in \bigcup_{n} \left[a_n, b_n\right]</math> in its domain then either <math>x_0</math> is equal to an endpoint of one of these intervals (that is, <math>x_0 \in \left\{a_1, b_1, a_2, b_2, \ldots\right\}</math>) or else there exists some index <math>n</math> such that <math>a_n < x_0 < b_n,</math> in which case <math>x_0</math> must be a point of discontinuity for <math>f\big\vert_{\left[a_n, b_n\right]}</math> (that is, <math>x_0 \in D_n</math>).
Thus the set <math>D</math> of all points of at which <math>f</math> is discontinuous is a subset of <math>\left\{a_1, b_1, a_2, b_2, \ldots\right\} \cup \bigcup_{n} D_n,</math> which is a countable set (because it is a union of countably many countable sets) so that its subset <math>D</math> must also be countable (because every subset of a countable set is countable).

In particular, because every interval (including open intervals and half open/closed intervals) of real numbers can be written as a countable union of closed and bounded intervals, it follows that any monotone real-valued function defined on an interval has at most countable many discontinuities.

To make this argument more concrete, suppose that the domain of <math>f</math> is an interval <math>I</math> that is not [[Closed set|closed]] and [[Bounded set|bounded]] (and hence by [[Heine–Borel theorem]] not [[Compact set|compact]]).
Then the interval can be written as a countable union of closed and bounded intervals <math>I_n</math> with the property that any two consecutive intervals have an [[Interval (mathematics)#Notations for intervals|endpoint]] in common: <math>I = \cup_{n=1}^\infty I_n.</math>
If <math>I = (a,b] \text{ with } a \geq -\infty</math> then <math>I_1 = \left[\alpha_1, b\right],\ I_2 = \left[\alpha_2, \alpha_1\right], \ldots, I_n = \left[\alpha_n, \alpha_{n-1}\right], \ldots</math> where <math>\left(\alpha_n\right)_{n=1}^{\infty}</math> is a strictly decreasing [[sequence]] such that <math>\alpha_n \rightarrow a.</math> In a similar way if <math>I = [a,b), \text{ with } b \leq +\infty</math> or if <math>I = (a,b) \text{ with } -\infty \leq a < b \leq \infty.</math>
In any interval <math>I_n,</math> there are at most countable many points of discontinuity, and since a countable union of at most countable sets is at most countable, it follows that the set of all discontinuities is at most countable.
<math>\blacksquare</math>

== Jump functions ==
'''Examples.''' Let {{mvar|''x''}}<sub>1</sub> < {{mvar|''x''}}<sub>2</sub> < {{mvar|''x''}}<sub>3</sub> < ⋅⋅⋅ be a countable subset of the compact interval [{{mvar|''a''}},{{mvar|''b''}}] and let μ<sub>1</sub>, μ<sub>2</sub>, μ<sub>3</sub>, ... be a positive sequence with finite sum. Set

:<math> f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mu_n \chi_{[x_n,b]} (x) </math>

where χ<sub>''A''</sub> denotes the [[indicator function|characteristic function]] of a compact interval {{mvar|''A''}}. Then {{mvar|''f''}} is a non-decreasing function on [{{mvar|''a''}},{{mvar|''b''}}], which is continuous except for jump discontinuities at {{mvar|''x''}}<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}</sub> for {{mvar|''n''}} ≥ 1. In the case of finitely many jump discontinuities, {{mvar|''f''}} is a '''[[step function]]'''. The examples above are generalised step functions; they are very special cases of what are called jump functions or saltus-functions.{{sfn|Apostol|1957}}{{sfn|Riesz|Sz.-Nagy|1990}}

More generally, the analysis of monotone functions has been studied by many mathematicians, starting from Abel, Jordan and Darboux. Following {{harvtxt|Riesz|Sz.-Nagy|1990}}, replacing a function by its negative if necessary, only the case of non-negative non-decreasing functions has to be considered. The domain [{{mvar|''a''}},{{mvar|''b''}}] can be finite or have ∞ or −∞ as endpoints.

The main task is to construct monotone functions — generalising step functions — with discontinuities at a given denumerable set of points and with prescribed left and right discontinuities at each of these points.
Let {{mvar|''x''<sub>''n''</sub>}} ({{mvar|''n''}} ≥ 1) lie in ({{mvar|''a''}}, {{mvar|''b''}}) and take λ<sub>1</sub>, λ<sub>2</sub>, λ<sub>3</sub>, ... and μ<sub>1</sub>, μ<sub>2</sub>, μ<sub>3</sub>, ... non-negative with finite sum and with λ<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}</sub> + μ<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}</sub> > 0 for each {{mvar|''n''}}. Define

:<math>f_n(x)=0\,\,</math> for <math>\,\, x < x_n,\,\, f_n(x_n) = \lambda_n, \,\, f_n(x) = \lambda_n +\mu_n\,\,</math> for <math>\,\, x > x_n.</math>

Then the '''jump function''', or '''saltus-function''', defined by

:<math> f(x)=\,\,\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x) =\,\, \sum_{x_n\le x} \lambda_n + \sum_{x_n<x} \mu_n,</math>

is non-decreasing on [{{mvar|''a''}}, {{mvar|''b''}}] and is continuous except for [[jump discontinuity|jump discontinuities]] at {{mvar|''x''<sub>''n''</sub>}} for {{mvar|''n''}} ≥ 1.<ref name="RSzN" />{{sfn|Saks|1937}}{{sfn|Natanson|1955}}{{sfn|Łojasiewicz|1988}}

To prove this, note that sup |{{mvar|''f''}}<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}</sub>| = λ<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}</sub> + μ<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}</sub>, so that Σ {{mvar|''f''}}<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}</sub> converges uniformly to {{mvar|''f''}}. Passing to the limit, it follows that

:<math>f(x_n)-f(x_n-0)=\lambda_n,\,\,\, f(x_n+0)-f(x_n)=\mu_n,\,\,\,</math> and <math>\,\, f(x\pm 0)=f(x)</math>

if {{mvar|''x''}} is not one of the {{mvar|''x''}}<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}</sub>'s.<ref name="RSzN" />

Conversely, by a differentiation theorem of [[Henri Lebesgue|Lebesgue]], the jump function {{mvar|''f''}} is uniquely determined by the properties:<ref>For more details, see
*{{harvnb|Riesz|Sz.-Nagy|1990}}
*{{harvnb|Young|Young|1911}}
*{{harvnb|von Neumann|1950}}
*{{harvnb|Boas|1961}}
*{{harvnb|Lipiński|1961}}
*{{harvnb|Rubel|1963}}
*{{harvnb|Komornik|2016}}
</ref> (1) being non-decreasing and non-positive; (2) having given jump data at its points of discontinuity {{mvar|''x''}}<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}</sub>; (3) satisfying the boundary condition {{mvar|''f''}}({{mvar|''a''}}) = 0; and (4) having zero derivative [[null set|almost everywhere]].

{{Collapse top|title=Proof that a jump function has zero derivative almost everywhere.|left=yes}}
Property (4) can be checked following {{harvtxt|Riesz|Sz.-Nagy|1990}}, {{harvtxt|Rubel|1963}} and {{harvtxt|Komornik|2016}}. Without loss of generality, it can be assumed that {{mvar|''f''}} is a non-negative jump function defined on the compact [{{mvar|''a''}},{{mvar|''b''}}], with discontinuities only in ({{mvar|''a''}},{{mvar|''b''}}).

Note that an open set {{mvar|''U''}} of ({{mvar|''a''}},{{mvar|''b''}}) is canonically the disjoint union of at most countably many open intervals {{mvar|''I''}}<sub>{{mvar|''m''}}</sub>; that allows the total length to be computed ℓ({{mvar|''U''}})= Σ ℓ({{mvar|''I''}}<sub>{{mvar|''m''}}</sub>). Recall that a null set {{mvar|''A''}} is a subset such that, for any arbitrarily small ε' > 0, there is an open {{mvar|''U''}} containing {{mvar|''A''}} with ℓ({{mvar|''U''}}) < ε'. A crucial property of length is that, if {{mvar|''U''}} and {{mvar|''V''}} are open in ({{mvar|''a''}},{{mvar|''b''}}), then ℓ({{mvar|''U''}}) + ℓ({{mvar|''V''}}) = ℓ({{mvar|''U''}} ∪ {{mvar|''V''}}) + ℓ({{mvar|''U''}} ∩ {{mvar|''V''}}).{{sfn|Burkill|1951|pp=10−11}} It implies immediately that the union of two null sets is null; and that a finite or countable set is null.<ref name="Ru">{{harvnb|Rubel|1963}}</ref><ref name="Ko">{{harvnb|Komornik|2016}}</ref>

'''Proposition 1.''' For {{mvar|''c''}} > 0 and a normalised non-negative jump function {{mvar|''f''}}, let {{mvar|''U''}}<sub>{{mvar|c}}</sub>({{mvar|''f''}}) be the set of points {{mvar|''x''}} such that

:<math>{f(t)-f(s)\over t -s} > c</math>

for some {{mvar|''s''}}, {{mvar|''t''}} with {{mvar|''s''}} < {{mvar|''x''}} < {{mvar|''t''}}. Then
{{mvar|''U''}}<sub>{{mvar|''c''}}</sub>({{mvar|''f''}}) is open and has total length ℓ({{mvar|''U''}}<sub>{{mvar|''c''}}</sub>({{mvar|''f''}})) ≤ 4 {{mvar|''c''}}<sup>−1</sup> ({{mvar|''f''}}({{mvar|''b''}}) – {{mvar|''f''}}({{mvar|''a''}})).

Note that {{mvar|''U''}}<sub>{{mvar|c}}</sub>({{mvar|''f''}}) consists the points {{mvar|''x''}} where the slope of {{mvar|''h''}} is greater that {{mvar|''c''}} near {{mvar|''x''}}. By definition {{mvar|''U''}}<sub>{{mvar|c}}</sub>({{mvar|''f''}}) is an open subset of ({{mvar|''a''}}, {{mvar|''b''}}), so can be written as a disjoint union of at most countably many open intervals {{mvar|''I''}}<sub>{{mvar|''k''}}</sub> = ({{mvar|''a''}}<sub>{{mvar|''k''}}</sub>, {{mvar|''b''}}<sub>{{mvar|''k''}}</sub>). Let {{mvar|''J''}}<sub>{{mvar|''k''}}</sub> be an interval with closure in {{mvar|''I''}}<sub>{{mvar|''k''}}</sub> and ℓ({{mvar|''J''}}<sub>{{mvar|''k''}}</sub>) = ℓ({{mvar|''I''}}<sub>{{mvar|''k''}}</sub>)/2. By compactness, there are finitely many open intervals of the form ({{mvar|''s''}},{{mvar|''t''}}) covering the closure of {{mvar|''J''}}<sub>{{mvar|''k''}}</sub>. On the other hand, it is elementary that, if three fixed bounded open intervals have a common point of intersection, then their union contains one of the three intervals: indeed just take the supremum and infimum points to identify the endpoints. As a result, the finite cover can be taken as adjacent open intervals ({{mvar|''s''}}<sub>{{mvar|''k'',1}}</sub>,{{mvar|''t''}}<sub>{{mvar|''k'',1}}</sub>), ({{mvar|''s''}}<sub>{{mvar|''k'',2}}</sub>,{{mvar|''t''}}<sub>{{mvar|''k'',2}}</sub>), ... only intersecting at consecutive intervals.<ref>This is a simple example of how [[Lebesgue covering dimension]] applies in one real dimension; see for example {{harvtxt|Edgar|2008}}.</ref> Hence
:<math>\ell(J_k) \le \sum_m (t_{k,m} - s_{k,m}) \le \sum_m c^{-1}(f(t_{k,m})-f(s_{k,m})) \le 2 c^{-1}(f(b_k)-f(a_k)).</math>
Finally sum both sides over {{mvar|''k''}}.<ref name="Ru"/><ref name="Ko"/>

'''Proposition 2.''' If {{mvar|''f''}} is a jump function, then {{mvar|''f''}} '({{mvar|''x''}}) = 0 almost everywhere.

To prove this, define

:<math>Df(x)= \limsup_{s,t\rightarrow x,\,\, s<x< t} {f(t)-f(s)\over t-s},</math>

a variant of the [[Dini derivative]] of {{mvar|''f''}}. It will suffice to prove that for any fixed {{mvar|''c''}} > 0, the Dini derivative satisfies {{mvar|''D''}}{{mvar|''f''}}({{mvar|''x''}}) ≤ {{mvar|''c''}} [[almost everywhere]], i.e. on a [[null set]].

Choose ε > 0, arbitrarily small. Starting from the definition of the jump function {{mvar|''f''}} = Σ {{mvar|''f''}}<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}</sub>, write {{mvar|''f''}} = {{mvar|''g''}} + {{mvar|''h''}} with {{mvar|''g''}} = Σ<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}≤{{mvar|''N''}}</sub> {{mvar|''f''}}<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}</sub> and {{var|''h''}} = Σ<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}>{{mvar|''N''}}</sub> {{mvar|''f''}}<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}</sub> where {{mvar|''N''}} ≥ 1. Thus {{mvar|''g''}} is a step function having only finitely many discontinuities at {{mvar|''x''}}<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}</sub> for {{mvar|''n''}} ≤ {{mvar|''N''}} and {{mvar|''h''}} is a non-negative jump function. It follows that {{mvar|''D''}}{{mvar|''f''}} = {{mvar|''g''}}' +{{mvar|''D''}}{{mvar|''h''}} = {{mvar|''D''}}{{mvar|''h''}} except at the {{mvar|''N''}} points of discontinuity of {{mvar|''g''}}. Choosing {{mvar|''N''}} sufficiently large so that Σ<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}>{{mvar|''N''}}</sub> λ<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}</sub> + μ<sub>{{mvar|''n''}}</sub> < ε, it follows that {{mvar|''h''}} is a jump function such that {{mvar|''h''}}({{mvar|''b''}}) − {{mvar|''h''}}({{mvar|''a''}}) < ε and {{mvar|''Dh''}} ≤ {{mvar|''c''}} off an open set with length less than 4ε/{{mvar|''c''}}.

By construction {{mvar|''Df''}} ≤ {{mvar|''c''}} off an open set with length less than 4ε/{{mvar|''c''}}. Now set ε' = 4ε/{{mvar|''c''}} — then ε' and {{mvar|''c''}} are arbitrarily small and {{mvar|''Df''}} ≤ {{mvar|''c''}} off an open set of length less than ε'. Thus {{mvar|''Df''}} ≤ {{mvar|''c''}} almost everywhere. Since {{mvar|''c''}} could be taken arbitrarily small, {{mvar|''Df''}} and hence also {{mvar|''f''}} ' must vanish almost everywhere.<ref name="Ru"/><ref name="Ko"/>
{{Collapse bottom}}
As explained in {{harvtxt|Riesz|Sz.-Nagy|1990}}, every non-decreasing non-negative function {{mvar|''F''}} can be decomposed uniquely as a sum of a jump function {{mvar|''f''}} and a continuous monotone function {{mvar|''g''}}: the jump function {{mvar|''f''}} is constructed by using the jump data of the original monotone function {{mvar|''F''}} and it is easy to check that {{mvar|''g''}} = {{mvar|''F''}} − {{mvar|''f''}} is continuous and monotone.<ref name="RSzN">{{harvnb|Riesz|Sz.-Nagy|1990|pp=13–15}}</ref>
